name: Fatima Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without ties to AI firms, employers or government. Your answers are confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach cello at a school in the morning, record short parts some afternoons and rehearse chamber music at night. I’m 27, lead our small ensemble and have a music master’s, though I still carry my own stands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what gets tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like hearing four players breathe together after a rough rehearsal. I get tired of moving between rooms and learning at the last moment whether a recording client has actually booked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my chamber players that AI Plateau might shorten the booking emails, but it would not change our rehearsals. I would ask the school to keep our lesson hours on the same written schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own pay would probably hold, though I keep three months of bills saved because freelance dates shift. I dislike handing a pupil’s recording to a tool I have not checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This Friday I’d confirm next term’s cello lessons with the school and keep the four chamber dates already booked. In the first year I’d put a fixed part of each paid recording fee into savings, provided the school hours stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly calm about the job in this picture. A cancelled concert would annoy me, but three months of expenses gives me room to repair the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a cancellation change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I share a flat with my partner, who works in a library. We could still pay rent while I tried to replace one cancelled date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a new booking tool if it were free?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the school secretary to show me the booking tool first. I have never used AI, and a pupil’s details deserve care. Three months of bills is a cushion, not a reason to risk someone else’s privacy.

say: I’d tell my **chamber players** that rehearsals and live dates still need us.
I would ask the **school** to keep cello lesson hours on a written schedule.
think: My **three-month cushion** can absorb one cancelled date while I look for another.
I will not hand a pupil’s **recording** to a tool I have not checked.
do: Confirm next term’s **cello lessons** with the school this Friday and keep four booked chamber dates.
Save part of each paid **recording fee** if school lesson hours remain steady.
feel: I feel **calm** about my work and rent because the cushion covers a missed concert.
fieldNote: Her **cushion** and partner’s library income reduce the force of one cancelled performance.
She wants a **demonstration** before using unfamiliar software and has never used AI herself.
S0.quote: Three months of bills is a cushion, not a reason to risk someone else’s privacy.

steps.text: Confirm school cello lessons and keep four booked chamber dates
Save part of each paid recording fee if school hours stay steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could take the small arrangements and booking messages off our desks before it touches the stage. I would ask the ensemble to keep paying players for rehearsals, not only performances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Private recording commissions help my income, and cheap generated parts could cut them. My school lessons feel steadier, but fewer commissions could still make me postpone a planned flat deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask three regular recording clients this month what work they still expect to hire me for. If two commissions disappear in the first year, I’d hold off on the flat deposit and offer one extra cello lesson slot only if the school has a room and a pupil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the recording fees because they fund the next step in my life. I would not panic over one bad month, but I would watch every contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much goes into that deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have saved roughly three months of living costs, but most of that is emergency money. I would not spend it on a flat deposit while commissions are falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the lessons were steady; why ask for more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A spare cello slot pays nothing until a pupil and a room both turn up. The school pays only for hours I actually teach.

say: I’d tell the ensemble that **arrangements** may move to software before live performances do.
I’d ask players to protect **paid rehearsals** as clients look for cheaper music.
think: Lost **recording commissions** could delay the flat deposit I planned with my partner.
School **lesson hours** feel safer, but pay arrives only for lessons actually taught.
do: Ask three **recording clients** this month what paid work they expect to keep.
Delay the **flat deposit** after two lost commissions and add one lesson only with a pupil and school room.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing income that was meant to move us into our own flat.
fieldNote: Her household remains solvent, but lost **commissions** could make a planned flat deposit unsafe.
The added **lesson** needs both a pupil and a room; she will not assume the school can supply either.
S1.quote: A spare cello slot pays nothing until a pupil and a room both turn up.

steps.text: Delay flat deposit if two recording commissions disappear
Add one school cello lesson if a pupil and room are available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the chamber group that AGI by 2028 could replace arranging, booking and much recorded music quickly. Robots that can play hands-on work as well as people would come around 2031, so live work has a different clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the studio might stop calling before the school does, though AI lessons could also challenge me in 2028. Three months of savings would not carry my share of rent through a long collapse in both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio for written dates this month and ask the school whether my teaching contract covers the next term. If recording calls stop in the first year after 2028, I’d cancel the rented practice room and teach from the school only if it approves the extra hours. If the school also cuts my hours, I would ask my partner to cover one month of bills, not a permanent share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about recording fees disappearing while I still have school lessons and three months saved. I’d be alarmed if the school cut my teaching hours as well. My cello case could leave the house every morning while the recording invoice book stays empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practice room has a monthly fee, so I could give notice and carry my cello to the school. My partner’s library wage would help keep our flat rent paid while I checked the next term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your partner to cover you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner’s library wage is steady but modest, and it cannot replace all my pay. I would ask for one month of help only if the school cut my hours too.

say: I’d warn the group that **thinking work** could change in 2028, before capable robots arrive around 2031.
I would ask for written **studio dates** rather than claim live bookings are safe.
think: The **studio** could stop calling before the school cuts lessons, but both incomes may be exposed.
Our household could not replace my whole **pay** with my partner’s modest library wage.
do: Ask the **studio** for written dates now and check the next school teaching contract.
Cancel the **practice room** after recording calls stop in 2028; take extra school hours only if approved.
Ask my **partner** for one month of help only if the school also cuts my teaching hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely lost recording fees and would be alarmed if school hours fell too.
fieldNote: She understands the **2028** threat to recorded and planning work and the later 2031 threat to live performance.
Extra school hours require **approval**; partner income and three months of savings do not cover a long double loss.
S2.quote: My cello case could leave the house every morning while the recording invoice book stays empty.

steps.text: Check studio dates and next school teaching contract now
Cancel rented practice room if recording calls stop after 2028
Ask partner for one month of help only if school hours also fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell pupils AGI by 2031 still leaves five years to learn how music teaching changes. Robots that can do hands-on playing as well as people would follow around 2034, so our ensemble has longer than the arranging side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me see whether families still pay for in-person lessons. I might keep my teaching post, but I cannot assume the recording money will survive 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d renew my school hours each term and ask the nearby arts centre this spring about an evening chamber class. If it has an open room and at least five paying players, I’d run one term; after 2031 I’d continue only while fees cover the room and my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious but less shaken than with the two-year date. I can ask for a real room and real names before promising my partner a bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to teach the class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use sheet music and live listening first. If a trusted colleague showed me a safe tool, I might look at it, but I would not promise to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the number five for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four chamber pupils would fill a room; five would pay for the room and my evening. I would cancel the class rather than ask four people to cover five places.

say: I’d tell pupils **teaching** can change by 2031 while capable performance robots arrive around 2034.
I’d ask the arts centre about a **chamber class** before promising one.
think: Five years lets me check whether families still buy **in-person lessons**.
I cannot count on **recording fees** once AGI can handle thinking work in 2031.
do: Renew **school hours** each term and ask the arts centre about an evening room this spring.
Run one **chamber term** only with a room and five paying players covering hire and time; continue after 2031 under that condition.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years allows me to test demand before moving home.
fieldNote: She makes the class conditional on **five fees** covering both room hire and her time.
Her refusal to promise **AI use** fits her resistant profile; she has not quietly adopted a tool.
S3.quote: Four chamber pupils would fill a room; five would pay for the room and my evening.

steps.text: Renew school cello lesson hours each term
Run chamber class with room and five paid players covering hire and time
Continue chamber class after 2031 only with five paid players covering room and time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my players AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to see which clients still want recorded and live music. Thinking work would face it in 2036; capable robots for hands-on playing would come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I might have stronger school hours and a home with my partner, if we save sensibly. I still would not borrow against the idea that every parent will keep paying for lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my teaching contract this year and set a separate flat fund from paid concert fees, but only after protecting three months of bills. In the first year after 2036, I’d check lesson enrollment before accepting a longer lease on teaching space. If my school hours fell, I would apply for a paid opening nearby and stay at the current school until an offer arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy rather than frightened by the long view. We have time to make ordinary choices, but I would still listen for the first cancelled commission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you split that money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first three months of expenses stay untouched; a new flat can wait for paid concerts. Fees above that reserve would go into a separate account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you change schools if hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are some other music posts nearby, so I would apply if a paid opening appeared. I would keep my present school hours until another school made an offer.

say: I’d tell players the **decade** gives time to watch which clients keep paying for music.
I would remind them that **thinking work** faces AGI in 2036 and capable robots follow around 2039.
think: I might build stronger **school hours** and a home with my partner by age 37.
I will not borrow against a **lesson market** that may change before 2036.
do: Keep the **school contract** this year and protect three months of expenses.
Save paid **concert fees** above the reserve for a flat; check enrollment before a longer space lease after 2036.
Apply for a nearby **paid post** if school hours fall, and keep current lessons until an offer arrives.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about cancellations but able to make measured plans over a decade.
fieldNote: Her **flat fund** begins only above a protected three-month reserve.
She would apply for another **paid post** if school hours fell, without leaving before an opening exists.
S4.quote: The first three months of expenses stay untouched; a new flat can wait for paid concerts.

steps.text: Keep current school cello contract and protect three months of expenses
Save paid concert fees above the reserve toward a flat
Apply for nearby paid school opening if hours fall; keep current lessons until offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because recorded work and lessons might both shrink before I can replace the income. Written school hours and affordable teaching space would help, provided families still enroll.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what I would protect first. I would keep the emergency savings untouched, because music bookings come and go even in an ordinary year.

headlineQuote: I would keep the emergency savings untouched, because music bookings come and go even in an ordinary year.
portrait: At **27**, Fatima leads a chamber ensemble, teaches cello and records parts after a music master’s degree.
Her typical **pay** and three-month reserve buffer a missed date, while recording fees still matter to housing plans.
She avoids unfamiliar **AI tools** and asks for demonstrations before risking pupil details.
She ties extra **teaching** to rooms, paying pupils and school approval across the faster AGI pictures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce recording work and lesson hours before she replaces either income.
whatWouldHelp: Written **school hours** and affordable teaching space would help if families still enroll.
